suggestions.rationale: Depressive symptoms and depressive disorders are common psychiatric comorbidities in adults with epilepsy/seizure disorders, but prevalence evidence does not establish that the seizure disorder caused an individual's depression. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis found a pooled depressive-symptom proportion of 40% across the cross-sectional studies included in its depression meta-analysis, with substantial heterogeneity. This mapping therefore supports association/comorbidity research only; seizure phenotype and control, antiseizure medications, chronology, sleep, cognition, psychosocial factors, and independent psychiatric causes require individual review.
evidenceGaps: Neurology documentation confirming the seizure/epilepsy diagnosis, phenotype, frequency, and control
Depressive-disorder diagnosis, severity, and chronology relative to seizure onset and treatment
Antiseizure medication history and possible mood effects
Sleep, cognitive, functional, psychosocial, and other psychiatric contributors
Qualified clinician assessment distinguishing common epilepsy/depression comorbidity from individual causation or aggravation

sourceReferences.citation: Rojas-López JC, Navas-Peñaranda S, Avilés-Gómez M, et al. Depression and anxiety in adults with epilepsy. Systematic literature review and meta-analysis. J Affect Disord. 2026;407:121741. PMID 41967683
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of adult epilepsy studies found a pooled depressive-symptom proportion of 40% in the cross-sectional depression meta-analysis, with high heterogeneity. Supports association/comorbidity research and screening relevance, not individual causal attribution.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 41967683; abstract Methods/Results/Conclusion: 54 studies extracted; depression meta-analysis 12 cross-sectional studies, n=3866; pooled depressive symptoms 40% (95% CI 30-50%)
